paragraphs: Katub gabbe shabbat (yeshaya nch, yg): "vekibbadto measot derakeka, mimmetzo cheptzeka vedabber dabar". vedareshu chaza"l (shabbat qyg, b) shello yihyeh dibbureka shel shabbat kedibbureka shel chol. vela mibbaya lomar lachabero laasot lo eseq peloni, deasur bazeh, mishshum daamira moelet laasiyya, deal yede amirato az, chabero oseh haeseq lemachar; ella apillu amira vedibbur sheen bahem toelet, kegon shemmedabber al atzmo veomer: dabar peloni eeseh lemachar, deap im lo yomar bepiv - hinneh hu oseh lemachar oto dabar, apillu hake asur, kol sheomer al asiyyat dabar sheasur laasoto bashshabbat; vaapillu im zeh hammaaseh enah melaka deorayeta, ella asura middibre soperim, g"k asur lomar beshabbat laasotah lemachar. veim hu debar mitzva, kegon sheomer beshabbat sherotzeh liktob lemachar s"t o tepillin umezuza vekayyotze bazeh, yesh mattirim mishshum decheptze shamayim hem, veyesh oserim, disbira lehu: lo ameru "cheptze shamayim muttarim ledabber bahem beshabbat", ella davqa im yesh tzorek lamtzuvva beoto dibbur, abal lomar: lemachar ektob tepillin umezuza - en tzorek beoto dibbur, deben im amar, ben im lo amar, hinneh hu oseh hammitzva lemachar, vetzarik lachush ledibre haoserin; mihu, katab harab "tosepet-shabbat" za"l, deim mityare shemma yitrashshel baddabar, shari lezaroze napsheh dehave keneder kemo shekkatab beyoreh dea, siman ra"n.

clarification.explanation: The verse concerning the Sabbath says, "from pursuing your affairs and speaking of them," and the Sages expounded from this that a person's speech on the Sabbath should not be like his speech on the weekdays. Therefore it is forbidden to tell one's friend to do a certain piece of business for him (since such a statement is of practical use — his friend will do it tomorrow as a result of his words). But even speech with no direct practical use — for example, a person saying to himself that he will do something specific tomorrow, even if he would have done it anyway without saying it — is forbidden to say aloud on the Sabbath, if it concerns something forbidden to do on the Sabbath, even if the prohibition is only rabbinic. If it concerns a matter of a commandment — for example, saying on the Sabbath that he wants to write a Torah scroll or tefillin and a mezuzah tomorrow — some permit this since it concerns "heavenly matters," and some forbid it, since in their view the permission to speak of heavenly matters on the Sabbath applies only when there is real need for that speech, but here there is no need for the speech itself, since whether he says it or not, he will do it tomorrow regardless; in practice one should be concerned for the stricter opinion, and should not say on the Sabbath that he will write tefillin tomorrow or the like. Nevertheless, if a person is concerned that he might become lazy and fail to carry out his intention, he is permitted to say it in order to strengthen his resolve, since this is similar to a vow.
takeaways: It is forbidden to speak on the Sabbath of doing work (even rabbinically forbidden work) to be done after the Sabbath, even if the speech has no direct practical use

Even for a matter of a commandment (such as "I will write tefillin tomorrow"), one should be concerned for the stricter opinion and not say it; only one who fears he might become lazy may say it to strengthen his resolve

paragraphs: Im tzarik lachabero o leezeh goy lesakeram bemotzae shabbat leezeh melaka, asur lomar lo beshabbat: "ba etzli laereb!" dachashib bazeh keillu medabber immo beperush lesakero, kevan shebbeemet bedato lesakero, veamar lo bilshon tzivvuy sheyyabo etzlo leareb; abal im eno omer lo bilshon tzivvuy, ella bederek sheela, sheomer lo: "hannireh beeneka shettabo etzli beereb?" – muttar, ap al pi shezzeh mebin shetztzarik lo lesakero limlaka.

clarification.explanation: One who wants to hire a person or a non-Jew at the conclusion of the Sabbath for a certain task is forbidden to say to him on the Sabbath, "Come to me in the evening!" in the form of a command, since this is considered as though he were explicitly discussing the hiring with him. But if he phrases it as a question, such as "Will you be able to come to me in the evening?" it is permitted, even though the other party understands that his intention is to hire him for work.
takeaways: One should not tell a person, in a commanding tone, to come for hire immediately at the conclusion of the Sabbath, but it is permitted to phrase it as a question, even if the intent to hire is clear

paragraphs: Muttar lomar lachabero: "likrak peloni ani holek lemachar", veken muttar lomar lo: "lek immi likrak peloni lemachar", kevan shehayyom hazzeh haya yakol lelek im hayu burganin badderek, parush: shomere sukkot, shekkol achat mublaat betok shibim amma vearbaa tepachim shel chabertah, deal yede kak yekolim lelek kamma parsaot beshabbat; v"p shebbeemet lo haya beoto shabbat burganin mimmeqomo leoto kerak - en issur haddabar bekak; veken kol kayyotze bazeh sheyyesh tzad hetter laasoto hayyom, yukal lomar lachabero sheyyaasennu lemachar; umihu, yizzaher shello yazkir bepiv leshon sekirut, shello yomar: "naskir lelek lemaqom peloni", o "nirkab lemaqom peloni al sus o baqqaron", kevan deen biskirut o rekiba hetter beshum open. veken im yesh lo debarim muqtzim bemaqom echad, asur lomar leacher sheyyebiem lemachar, mippene shehem asurim letaltel beshabbat. veasur name lehachshik besop hattechum kede sheyyemaher lelek lesham ballayla lahabiam; mihu, katab harab "tosepet-shabbat", deperot sheenam muqtzim, apillu shehem rechoqim harbeh beinyan shello haya epshar lahabiam beshabbat mechamat richuq hammaqom, muttar lomar leacher lahabiam lo lemachar, kevan deen issur shabbat gorem lo lebilti yebiem hayyom, ki im richuq hammaqom hu hammonea biatam hayyom, velaken muttar lomar lahabiam lemachar.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to say to one's friend, "Tomorrow I am going to such-and-such a city," and likewise it is permitted to say, "Come with me tomorrow to such-and-such a city," since it would have been possible in principle to go there already today (on the Sabbath) had there been "burganin" (guard posts spaced apart at the permitted carrying distance, enabling long-distance walking on the Sabbath) along the way — and this is so even if in fact there were none on this particular route. So too in any similar case where there is a theoretical side of permission to do it today, it is permitted to tell one's friend that he will do it tomorrow. But one must be careful not to mention language of hiring, such as "let us hire [transport] to go to such-and-such a place" or "let us ride a horse or wagon to such-and-such a place," since in hiring or riding there is no side of permission at all. Likewise, if he has muktzeh items in another place, it is forbidden to tell his friend to bring them to him tomorrow, since they are forbidden to be carried on the Sabbath itself. He may also not wait until the end of the Sabbath boundary in order to hurry and go fetch them immediately at the conclusion of the Sabbath. But fruits that are not muktzeh, even if they are too far away to bring on the Sabbath (because of the distance and not because of a prohibition), may be mentioned to a friend to bring tomorrow, since what prevents bringing them today is the distance and not a Sabbath prohibition.
takeaways: It is permitted to plan and speak of tomorrow's travel if there is some theoretical side of permission to do it on the Sabbath itself — but one should not mention language of hiring or riding, which have no such permission at all
It is forbidden to speak of bringing muktzeh items tomorrow, but permitted to speak of bringing fruits (not muktzeh) that only distance prevents from being brought today

paragraphs: Apillu besichat debarim betelim sheen bahem zeker asiyyat melaka kelal, asur leharbot beshabbat, kede shello yihyeh dibburo beshabbat kedibburo bechol. ubene-adam shessippure maasiyyot ushemuot vedibre chiddushim oneg lahem, muttarim lesapper beshabbat, abal en lahem leharbot besichot ellu. umi shechosheb al melaka beyom shabbat laasotah bechol, enah mitbareket, kevan shechashab aleha beshabbat vekannizkar b"chesed laalapim"; veayyen "kap-hachayyim", dap ry"ch.

clarification.explanation: Even idle chatter that contains no hint of doing work should not be indulged in excessively on the Sabbath, so that speech on the Sabbath not be like speech on weekdays. Nevertheless, people who enjoy stories, news, and novel remarks are permitted to tell them on the Sabbath, but not to excess. One who thinks in his mind, during the Sabbath, about work he will do during the week — that work will not be blessed, since he thought about it on the Sabbath.
takeaways: It is permitted to tell stories and novel remarks on the Sabbath for enjoyment, but not to excess
Thinking about weekday work during the Sabbath harms the blessing of that work when it is done

paragraphs: Asur lachshob cheshbonotayv - ben cheshbon heatid lihyot, ben cheshbon sheabar kebar, ella shetztzarik lihyot lo atta leda oto, kegon: kak vekak hotzeti al binyan peloni biskirut happoalim, vehu adayin lo asa cheshbon immahem qodem shabbat, velo yada im maggia lahem od etzlo o kamma yaggia lahem od, velaken asur, denimtza yesh lo tzorek atta bazeh hacheshbon shehu mechashsheb "p shehu kebar abar; v"p sheatta baasoto hacheshbon beno leben atzmo matza sheeno chayyab lahem kelum, im kol zeh, hare qodem haya mistappeq, veatta nitbarer lo, venimtza yesh lo bazeh tzorek veasur. veken apillu shehu lo haya lo tzorek beoto cheshbon kelal shekkebar asa cheshbon immahem, veraq chozer vechosheb hahotzaa shel habbinyan sheasa kede lehodia laacherim sheyyesh lahem tzorek bidia zo, sheggam hem rotzim laasot binyan kazeh, uretzonam leda kamma tzarik lahem, hare zeh asur; abal cheshbonot sheaberu sheen tzorek bahem kelal, lo lo velo laacherim, veraq hu mazkir otam beshabbat besippur debarim bealema, muttar; velaken muttar lachshob kamma seim tebua haya lo bashshana sheabera, vekamma massaot shalach lair peloni, vekamma dinarim hotzi al beto, vekayyotze bazeh bidbarim sheen tzorek bahem atta, lo lahem velo laacherim; ak tzarik lizzaher shello leharbot bidbarim ellu. vekatab haggaon chida" za"l b"moreh beetzba", ot qn": hagam deyesh mattirim becheshbonot sheaberu - yesh oserin, veshomer napsho yirchaq mehem; vehen, lu yehi deshare - mizzeh yabo ledabar haggorem leatid, al ken yistom happetach vetob lo; yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to calculate accounts on the Sabbath — both a future account and a past account that one needs to know now. For example: one who spent money on a building and hired workers, and has not yet made a final accounting with them before the Sabbath, and does not know whether he still owes them money — he is forbidden to calculate this on the Sabbath, since he has a real practical need for it (even if it turns out in the end that he owes nothing). Likewise, if he has already made the accounting and finished it, but goes back to think about the building expenses in order to tell others for a practical purpose (such as, they too want to build a similar building and want to know the cost) — this too is forbidden. But past accounts that serve no need, either for him or for others, and are mentioned only as idle conversation, are permitted. For example, it is permitted to say how much produce he had last year, how many shipments he sent, how much he spent on his house, and the like — as long as there is no practical need for it, though even this should not be done to excess. There is a stricter opinion (the Chida) that even needless past accounts should preferably be avoided, so as not to be led from there into speech that has a future need.
takeaways: It is forbidden to calculate accounts that serve a practical need (future, or an unresolved past matter), but it is permitted to mention past figures as mere idle conversation with no practical need — provided one does not do so excessively

paragraphs: Asur lomar lachabero: bekak vekak qaniti chepetz zeh o keli zeh, im yodea bachabero sherotzeh gam hu liqnot mimmennu, deaz yesh lo tzorek leda erek hachepetz, vedabar zeh matzuy ben ish lereehu, ben ishsha lirotah, laken tzarik lehazhir bazeh et haanashim veet hannashim; abal im en tzorek lachabero bidia zo, hare zeh sippur debarim bealema umuttar mishshurat haddin; velaken muttar lomar: kak vekak hotzeti bachatunna, vekak vekak hotzeti babbinyan vekayyotze bazeh. veasur ledabber dabar shezzoker lo tzaaro.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to tell one's friend how much a particular item or utensil cost him, if it is known that the friend is planning to buy something similar — since he then has a practical need to know the price, and this situation applies to both men and women, so both should be cautioned about it. But if the friend has no real need for this information, it is mere idle conversation and is permitted by strict law — for example, it is permitted to say how much one spent on a wedding or a building and the like. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to speak of matters that remind one's friend of his grief.
takeaways: It is forbidden to speak of prices on the Sabbath if the friend himself is planning to buy something similar and has a practical need for the information, but it is permitted as mere conversation when there is no such need
One should not speak of topics that cause the listener grief

paragraphs: Shitre chobot vekayyotze, veken iggerot shekkebar qeraam, asur liqrot bahem; vaapillu leayyen bahem asur, vahare hem muqtzim deasur letaltelam; abal iggeret shello qarea adayin, velo yada mah katub bah, muttar lepatechah "y goy uleayyen bah, deshemma yesh bah debarim shehem tzareke haggup. veim yesh betokah pitqaot shel cheshbonot, lo yeayyen bahem kelal. veiggeret zo hachadasha deamarnu muttar liqrotah - haynu leayyen bah, abal lo yotzi haddebarim mippiv im hem debarim shel massa umattan; veachar sheyyiqraenna paam achat, shub asur leayyen bah paam shenit, ella yatznienna bemaqom acher, deaz naaset etzlo muqtzeh. venahagu shello leqabbel haiggeret miyyad hannakeri hammebia beshabbat, ella omerim lo sheyyannichenna al gab qarqa o al gab hashshulchan, dechosheshin shemma terem sheyyaamod hannakeri lapush, yittol hayisrael haiggeret miyyado, venimtza hayisrael oseh hannacha, veasur middibre soperim ap bazzeman hazzeh, sheyyesh omerim deen lanu din reshut harabbim; ukemo shekkatab haggaon rabbi zalman beshulchan aruk, seip k"ch; veayyen "kap-hachayyim", dap rk"t.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to read promissory notes and letters that have already been read, and even merely glancing at them is forbidden, since they are considered muktzeh and forbidden to be handled. But a letter not yet read, whose contents are unknown, may be given to a non-Jew to open and examine, in case it contains matters relevant to a person's physical needs (such as medical or important information). If it contains account slips, they should not be examined at all. The new letter may only be examined; its contents should not be spoken aloud if he is engaged in negotiations. After it has been read once, it may not be examined again, but should be set aside elsewhere, since it becomes muktzeh. It is customary not to receive a letter that a non-Jew brings on the Sabbath directly from his hand, but rather to ask him to place it on the ground or on the table, out of concern that the Jew might take it from his hand before the non-Jew has finished his business — which would be considered a forbidden "placing" (hanachah) by rabbinic law. This prohibition remains firmly in force by rabbinic decree even today, even though some say we no longer have a full public domain by Torah law (which might have been lenient regarding "hanachah") — since even according to them the rabbinic prohibition remains in place.
takeaways: One should not read or examine notes and letters already read (they are muktzeh), but a new, unread letter may be opened (by a non-Jew) and examined — only once
One should not receive a letter directly from a non-Jew's hand on the Sabbath, but should ask him to place it on a surface
The prohibition on receiving an item from a non-Jew's hand ("hanachah") applies rabbinically even today, even for those who hold there is no full public domain today

paragraphs: Mi sherotzeh lezammen orechim lasseuda beshabbat, vekoteb shemotam meereb shabbat lemazkeret, kede shello yishkach leqaream beshabbat; veken abi habben o hechatan shemmezammen ohabayv uqerobayv laaliyyat s"t beshabbat, vekoteb shemotam meereb shabbat - asur lebaal hasseuda atzmo o abi habben vehechatan liqrot biktab zeh beshabbat, degazeru chaza"l (shabbat qmt, ) shemma yimchoq shem echad min haqqeruim asher nicham alayv sheeno rotzeh leqareo; vegam gezera shemma yiqra beshitre hedyotot; abal hashshammash muttar leechoz uleayyen biktab hareshima shel shemot haanashim hahem kede leqaream, deen shayyak bo gezera shemma yimchoq; veap-al-gab deit beh mishshum: shemma yiqra beshitre hedyotot, apillu hake nahagu haolam hetter bazeh shehashshammash qore mittok hakketab hazzeh shemot hamzummanim, dachashib tzareke metzuvveh, velo gazeru bazeh mishshum: yiqra beshitre hedyotot; mihu, achar shehishlim hashshammash melakto veqara bo hamzummanim, asur lo liqrot uleayyen bo od beshabbat. veken mah shennahagu hashshammash qore bebet-hakkeneset ketab hakraza shel haskamot vetiqqune hair shemmakrizin habbet-din uparnesi haqqahal, mishshum detzareke rabbim chashibi tzareke metzuvveh; veachar hakraza, lo yiqreu viayyenu od bo bayyom.

clarification.explanation: One who wants to invite guests to a Sabbath meal and wrote down their names before the Sabbath so as not to forget to invite them, and likewise the father of a boy being circumcised or a groom who wrote before the Sabbath the names of those to be called to the Torah — it is forbidden for the host, the father, or the groom himself to read from this list on the Sabbath, out of concern that he might cross out the name of one of the invitees whom he has reconsidered, and also out of concern that he might come to read ordinary documents. But the attendant (who has no personal stake in the list) is permitted to hold and examine the list in order to call the people, since there is no concern that he will cross out a name — and the concern about reading ordinary documents does not apply here either, since this is considered a need for a commandment. But once the attendant has finished his task and called all the invitees, he may not go back and examine the list again that same day. Similarly, it is customary for the synagogue attendant to read announcements and rulings of the court and the community leaders, since this too is considered a need for a commandment — but after the announcement, he may not go back and examine the document again that same day.
takeaways: The host or the celebrant may not himself read the guest list on the Sabbath, but the attendant may read it for the sake of the commandment — only once
Similarly, the attendant may read community announcements for the sake of a commandment, but not review the document again afterward that day

paragraphs: Kol dabar sheasur leyisrael laasoto beshabbat, asur lomar lenakeri laasoto, vaapillu beremez; vaapillu sheeno romez lo bidbarim, ella romez lo beyadayv beezeh tenua; vaapillu ramaz lenakeri sheyyomar lenakeri acher leakkeb hannakeri beshabbat bishbil hachob, asur; abal muttar lomar bechol lashshopet hannakeri: maddua lo ikkabta hannakeri beshabbat sheabera? ap-al-pi shemmebin mittok debarayv sheyyeakkebennu bashshabbatot habbaim im yizdammen az lair. mihu, mi sheyyesh lo chob etzel goy, venoda lo beshabbat sheyyelek min hair veepshar shello yashub od, muttar lelek beshabbat liqbol lipne hammoshel sheyyipraennu, debimqom peseda lo gazeru; ak im tzarik lehabi et shetar chobo lipne hammoshel, lo yetaltel hashshetar beyado, ella yiqqach immo goy vehu yetaltel hashshetar veyirennu lemoshel; veim epshar laasot gam haqqublana "y haggoy – hinneh mah tob. veim tzarik laabor bispina qetanna – ap-al-gab deharab "chayye-adam" za"l katab beheka deikka hepsed barur im lo yaabor, yesh lehattir, nireh li dela arik lehorot ken: chada laabor bispina beshabbat avesha milleta, veyesh bazeh chillul-hashshem lipne haggoyim; veod yesh bazeh issur mishshum marit haayin, deharoeh chosheb sheyyored letayyel, veshanya da mehak dina deqabbelana.

clarification.explanation: Anything forbidden for a Jew to do himself on the Sabbath is also forbidden to tell a non-Jew to do, even by mere hint — whether a verbal hint or a hint by hand gesture. Even hinting to one non-Jew to tell another non-Jew to detain a person over a debt is forbidden. But it is permitted to say, during the week, to a non-Jewish judge, "Why didn't you detain that non-Jew last Sabbath?" — even though it is clear from his words that he is hinting for him to detain him on future Sabbaths as well. One who is owed a debt by a non-Jew, and learns on the Sabbath that the non-Jew is about to leave the city and may not return — is permitted to go on the Sabbath and approach the authorities to collect the debt, since the Sages were not stringent when it comes to preventing an actual loss. But if he needs to bring the promissory note with him, he should not carry it himself, but have a non-Jew carry and return the note. If the entire claim can be handled by the non-Jew alone, this is preferable. If he must cross by a small boat to get there, Rabbi Yosef Chaim disagrees with a lenient opinion (Chayei Adam) that permitted this in a case of clear loss, since this involves a desecration of God's name in the eyes of the non-Jews (who see a Jew sailing on the Sabbath) and an appearance of impropriety (since it looks like he is merely strolling); therefore one should not rule leniently on this, even though the claim itself was permitted in this case.
takeaways: It is forbidden to hint to a non-Jew to do on the Sabbath something forbidden to a Jew, but in a case of preventing a real monetary loss, one may approach the authorities to collect a debt — though not by sailing a boat, out of concern for desecration of God's name and appearance of impropriety

paragraphs: Im haggoy haya tapus bebet haasurim bishbil yehudi shechayyab lo, muttar lomar hayyehudi lemoshel leqabbel arbut acher, abal lo yomar lo sheyyiktob zot bearkaot; abal im hammoshel meatzmo koteb, en lachush; vezeh davqa beheka sheyyabo lide peseda, abal im lekka peseda, asur; gam asur leakkeb nikse reuben beyad shimon beshabbat.

clarification.explanation: If a non-Jew is detained in prison over a debt owed to a Jew, the Jew is permitted to tell the authorities to accept a different guarantor in place of the imprisoned non-Jew, but he may not ask the authorities to formally record this in court. If the authorities record it on their own initiative, there is no problem. This permission applies only when there is concern of monetary loss; if there is no such concern, it is forbidden. Likewise, it is forbidden to have someone's assets detained in another person's hands on the Sabbath.
takeaways: It is permitted to ask the authorities on the Sabbath to release a non-Jewish debtor in exchange for a different guarantor, only if there is concern of monetary loss, and one may not request formal court registration

paragraphs: Im yesh liruben al adam echad "polisa" (hamchaa) shebbaa lo meir acheret al adam echad lizman yadua, vezeh haadam shebbaa alayv ha"polisa" lo para bizman happeraon; veim reuben lo yelek beyom shabbat lebet vaad shel hattaggarim laasot "poratisato" (tebia mishpatit), lo yukal litboa hammaot min koteb ha"polisa" – hinneh shurat haddin bazeh hu: i ikka peseda, kegon shezzeh shebbaa alayv ha"polisa" eno amud, veepshar shehu meshubbar gam-ken, az muttar liruben laleket lebet vaad hattaggarim lehodia hainyan, veyabi goy echad, vehu yiqqach et ha"polisa" beyado veyirenna lerosh bet vaad hattaggarim, vehu lo yomar lo sheyyiktob lo "poratisato", ella hu yaaseh middato bevadday; veim epshar shello yelek hu kelal, ella hakkol yaaseh al-yede goy – hinneh mah tob; veim lekka peseda, kegon shezzeh haadam shennitchayyeb b"polisa" hu amud, shebbevadday yipra achar-kak, asur leyisrael laasot dabar zeh beshabbat, ap-al-pi sheal-yede kak yeabbed koach zekut sheyyesh lo bezo ha"polisa" al adam hakkoteb otah.

clarification.explanation: If Reuven has a promissory note ("policy") that came from another place, on a certain person who was supposed to pay it by a fixed time, and that person did not pay on time — and if Reuven does not go on the Sabbath to the merchants' council to file a claim, he will not be able to claim the money from the writer of the note — the law is: if there is real concern of loss (for example, if the debtor lacks means and might even go bankrupt), Reuven is permitted to go to the merchants' council to report the matter, but he should do so through a non-Jew, who should carry the note and show it to the head of the council, without Reuven explicitly asking the non-Jew to file the claim — rather, the non-Jew should do so on his own initiative. If the whole matter can be handled entirely by the non-Jew, this is preferable. But if there is no concern of loss (the debtor has means and will clearly pay eventually), it is forbidden for the Jew to do this on the Sabbath, even if as a result he loses the right to claim from the writer of the note.
takeaways: Only when there is real concern of monetary loss is it permitted to approach (through a non-Jew) the merchants' council on the Sabbath regarding an unpaid note — and even then, one should not explicitly ask the non-Jew to file the claim

paragraphs: Im ba lo ketab b"telagrep" (mibbaraq) beyom-shabbat, vehaggoy lo yimsor oto leyisrael ella ad sheyyachtom bechotam shello al neyar haqqabbala sheyyabi lo kannahug – heeleti besiyyata dishmayya besipri haqqadosh "rab-berakot", dap qmv, sheyyihyeh etzel yisrael mezumman umukan chotem bishmo hakkatub biktab yishmeelim o ketiba acheret, beopen sheen bo ketiba ashshurit; ukesheyyabi lo haggoy et ha"telagrep", qodem sheyyimserennu leyado yannicha lipne haggoy et hachotam hahu bishtiqa, vehaggoy mebin meatzmo veyiqqach hachotam meal haqqarqa veyachtom bo et neyar haqqabbala veyelek lo.

clarification.explanation: If a telegram arrives on the Sabbath, and the non-Jewish messenger insists on delivering it only if the Jew signs a receipt — Rabbi Yosef Chaim wrote in his book Rav Berachot that one should prepare in advance a stamp with the Jew's name in Arabic script or another script that is not Ashuri script (the sacred Hebrew script), and place it silently in front of the non-Jew before he delivers the telegram — and the non-Jew will understand on his own and take the stamp and sign the receipt himself.
takeaways: When a non-Jew requires a signature on a receipt to deliver a telegram on the Sabbath, this is resolved by silently placing a stamp (in non-Ashuri script) so that the non-Jew signs it himself, without the Jew acting or speaking

paragraphs: Im ba lo iggeret chatuma, muttar litten otah lenakeri lepatechah, ubilbad shello yomar lo "tiptachna!" ella moserah beyado vehu mebin meatzmo dabar zeh veyiptachenna. veyesh omerim, im lo hebin haggoy dabar zeh liptoach otah meatzmo, muttar lomar lo: en ani yakol liptoach iggeret zo beshabbat! kede sheyyabin haggoy veyiptachenna; ki beinyan zeh shel petichat haiggeret yesh tzedadim lehaqel beremez, vehake nahug.

clarification.explanation: If a sealed letter arrives, it is permitted to hand it to a non-Jew so that he opens it, provided one does not explicitly tell him, "Open it!" but merely hands him the letter silently, and the non-Jew understands on his own and opens it. Some say that if the non-Jew does not understand this on his own, it is permitted to say to him, "I cannot open this letter on the Sabbath!" — so that the non-Jew understands and opens it himself, since regarding the opening of a letter there are grounds to be lenient by way of a hint, and this is indeed the custom.
takeaways: It is permitted to hand a sealed letter to a non-Jew to open, preferably without saying anything, or at most with an indirect hint that is not a direct command

paragraphs: Asur litten maot meereb-shabbat liqnot lo beshabbat; veken asur litten lo peraqmatya limkor lo beshabbat, abal im lo amar lo liqnot o limkor beshabbat, ella natan lo bime hachol bistam, ap-al-pi shezzeh hannakeri qoneh o moker beshabbat, muttar; ubilbad sheyyiqtzotz lo sekar tarecho kede sheyyehe hannakeri addata denapshah qaabed. veha dehittarnu beqatzatz benoten lo bistam veeno omer lo beshabbat, haynu davqa beheka deepshar lenakeri liqnot o limkor zeh bime hachol, abal im i epshar lo liqnot o limkor ella davqa beshabbat, kemo meqomot sheyyom hashshuq shellahem hu beyom shabbat davqa, az apillu im amar lo bistam velo hizkir lo yom-shabbat, vaapillu sheqqatzatz lo sekar tarecho memot hachol, asur, kevan dei epshar liqnot velimkor zeh ella beshabbat, hava lah keillu amar lo beperush liqnot o limkor beshabbat. veap-al-pi shebbeseper "rab-berakot" hittarti bikhay gavna benoten lo bistam veeno mazkir lo shabbat – lo hittarti bazeh ella baabur tzorek gadol meod, shehashshoel haya mukrach meod bedabar zeh, sheim lo yeaseh ken yatza lo nezeq gadol, velaken samakti sham al hammattirim bikhay gavna, beheka deqatzatz veomer lo bistam sheeno mazkir shabbat kelal, abal bilti letzorek gadol meod en lehattir, ki rabbu haoserim. vehinneh poh irenu bagdad y" nimtza inyan kazeh shehu tzorek gadol meod, sheshsholechim mikkan leir acheret bispinat qitor tzerorot kesep o zahab, vehassepina holeket beyom sheni, veah"qepatan" (rab chobel) eno meqabbel tzerorot ella raq beyom shabbat, ki beyom rishon hu ed shello; vegam beereb-shabbat lo yeqabbel, mippene sheoto hayyom higgia hassepina. veyesh socharim shetztzerikin lishloach tzerorot kesep lebatzera o lebomebbe, veyesh lahem tzorek gadol meod bazeh, mippene shehem makeru "polisa" al happaqid shellahem bebatzera o bebomebbe, veim lo yishlechu lo tzerorot hakkesep, yatza lahem nezeq gadol sheyyachazir ha"polisa", o yesh od tzorek acher gadol meod; al-ken gam bazeh yesh lehattir sheyyimsor hayisrael et tzeror hakkesep beyad haggoy sheyyishlachennu bispina, veyiqtzotz lo sekar tarecho bazeh, velo yomar lo sheyyeshallechenna beyom shabbat, ella yomar lo sheyyeshallechenna bistam, veap-al-pi shehu yodea shezzeh yishlachenna beyom shabbat, ki i epshar sheyyeqabbel ha"qptn" tzerorot ella raq beyom shabbat – im kol zeh, kevan shehu tzorek gadol meod, sheyyatza lo nezeq im lo yishlach hatztzeror beotah sepina, yesh lismok al hammattirin bazeh; vegam yesh tzad yoter lehaqel bazeh – deshemma yihyeh ikkub lassepina shello telek ella beyom shelishi, veaz ha"qptn" yodia sheyyeqabbel tzerorot beyom sheni, o yivvaled open acher shello yitztarek haggoy leholik hatztzeror beshabbat, abal bilti tzorek gadol kazeh, en lehattir.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to give a non-Jew money before the Sabbath so that he buys something for him on the Sabbath itself, and likewise it is forbidden to give him merchandise to sell on the Sabbath. But if one did not explicitly tell him to buy or sell specifically on the Sabbath, but gave it to him during the week without specifying, and the non-Jew nevertheless chooses to buy or sell on the Sabbath — this is permitted, provided a fee was set in advance so that the non-Jew acts on his own initiative and for his own purposes. But this permission (giving it unspecified and setting a fee) applies only if the non-Jew can also buy or sell during the week; if he can only buy or sell on the Sabbath (for example, in places where their market day is specifically the Sabbath), it is forbidden, since this resembles an explicit instruction to do it on the Sabbath. Rabbi Yosef Chaim describes a special case in his city of Baghdad: when money or gold needs to be sent by steamship to another city, and the ship's captain accepts parcels only on the Sabbath (since Sunday is his holiday, and he does not accept them on Friday either, since that day the ship arrives at port and he is busy) — if there is a very great need (such as concern for significant business loss due to the money not being delivered in time), it is permitted to hand the parcel of money to the non-Jew unspecified, without explicitly telling him "send it on the Sabbath," and to set a fee for him — even though it is clear that he will send it specifically on the Sabbath, since there is no other option. But this permission applies only for a very great need, not casually. It should be noted that there is also an additional lenient consideration here, since the matter is not entirely certain: perhaps the ship will be delayed and depart only on Tuesday, in which case the captain will announce that he accepts parcels already on Monday, or another way will be found by which the non-Jew will not need to carry the parcel specifically on the Sabbath — so there is also an element of doubt supporting the lenient side, though this too was said only in a case of very great need, not casually.
takeaways: It is permitted to give a non-Jew money or merchandise during the week unspecified (without mentioning the Sabbath), with a fixed fee, even if the non-Jew ends up buying or selling on the Sabbath — but if it can only be done on the Sabbath, this is forbidden except in a case of very great loss
There is also an element of doubt supporting the lenient side in a case of great need (the ship might be delayed, or an alternative route found that avoids sending specifically on the Sabbath)

paragraphs: Goy sheqqana sechora miyyisrael, uba lelaqecha beshabbat mibbet yisrael, apillu beyesh erub, asur, kede shello yachsheduhu shemmekarah lo beshabbat. veken hu haddin chammarim o gemallim shessakar etzlam laset lo massaot meereb-shabbat, deasur lehannicham labo lebeto beshabbat lehotzi hammassaot, ap-al-pi sheqqatzatz, venakeri addatah denapshah qaabed, im kol zeh asur mippene hachashad, deavesha milleta.

clarification.explanation: A non-Jew who bought merchandise from a Jew and comes to take it from his house on the Sabbath — it is forbidden to give it to him, even if there is an eruv, out of concern that people will suspect the Jew of having sold him the merchandise on the Sabbath itself. The same applies to donkeys or camels that the Jew hired before the Sabbath to carry loads for him — it is forbidden to let them come to his house on the Sabbath to take out the loads, even if he set the fee in advance (which generally permits a non-Jew to act for his own purposes), since here there is concern about people's suspicion (that they will think the Jew conducted business on the Sabbath).
takeaways: Merchandise or loads should not be handed over to a non-Jew from the house on the Sabbath, even with a fee set in advance, out of concern that people will suspect a business transaction took place on the Sabbath

paragraphs: Hashshoel mechabero dabar beshabbat veeno maamino, yakol lehannicha mashkon etzlo, ak yannicha hammashkon bistam velo yomar lo beperush: "helak mashkon zeh!" dezehu kemaaseh chol. bammeh debarim amurim? beshoel mine maakol umashqeh o malbush shehem letzorek hashshabbat, abal shello letzorek hashshabbat, asur lehannicha mashkon, sheddomeh lammaqneh qinyan beshabbat.

clarification.explanation: One who borrows an item from his friend on the Sabbath, and the friend does not trust that he will return it, may leave a pledge with him — but he should leave it unspecified, without explicitly saying, "Here is a pledge for you!" since such a statement is considered a weekday commercial act. This law applies specifically when the borrowing is of food, drink, or clothing needed for the Sabbath itself; but if the borrowing is not for the sake of the Sabbath, it is forbidden to leave a pledge, since this resembles creating a commercial transaction on the Sabbath.
takeaways: It is permitted to leave a pledge (silently, without an explicit statement) when borrowing an item for the sake of the Sabbath itself, but not when the borrowing is not for the sake of the Sabbath

paragraphs: Dabar shehu melaka min hattora, asur lomar laggoy laasoto bashshabbat apillu letzorek metzuvveh, abal dabar sheissuro middibre soperim, muttar lomar beshabbat laasoto letzorek metzuvveh uletzorek choli, apillu choli sheeno kolel kol haggup veeno sakkanat ebar; veyesh mattirin gam ken bimqom hepsed, kegon letaltel "y nakeri sechora muqtzet hannipsedet baggeshamim, veyesh lismok al dibrehem behepsed gadol.

clarification.explanation: Something that is a Torah-forbidden act of labor may not be told to a non-Jew to do on the Sabbath, even for the sake of a commandment. But something whose prohibition is only rabbinic may be told to a non-Jew to do on the Sabbath for the sake of a commandment or for the sake of a sick person, even a sick person whose condition is not life-threatening or limb-threatening (a relatively minor illness). Some also permit this in a case of monetary loss, such as asking a non-Jew to carry muktzeh merchandise that might be damaged by rain, and one may rely on this opinion when the loss is great.
takeaways: Something forbidden only rabbinically (unlike a Torah prohibition) may be asked of a non-Jew to do on the Sabbath for the sake of a commandment, a sick person, or a case of great monetary loss

paragraphs: "p shehirhur baasaqayv muttar, yesh hirhur deasur middina, kegon shemmehallek beshabbat besadehu o bemaqom shel eseq melaka sheosin sham poalin shello bechol, kede lirot mah tzerika sadehu o meqom hammelaka achar hashshabbat. v"p sheshsham eno medabber kelum bo bayyom ella raq mechashsheb belibbo, hare zeh asur middina, yaan kevan sheoseh maaseh hahalika beshabbat lemaqom sheen lo tzorek bo bayyom hashshabbat - minnakra milleta sheholek lirot lehazmin bedato dabar sheasur laasoto bashshabbat; deim lo ken, mah tzorek yesh lo bahalikato sham bo bayyom? veken hu haddin im metayyel bair bemaqom dishkichi sham susim vachamorim, o bimqom sepinot o qeronot, lirot ezeh sus o qaron o sepina haarbayim lo kede lesakeram lemachar, deminnakra milleta debaabur zot halak letayyel sham, diblav haki lo haya holek letayyel sham; degam bikhay gavna ikka issura, "p sheeno medabber veeno oseh bo bayyom dabar haasur lo, veken kol kayyotze bazeh.

clarification.explanation: Even though mental reflection on business matters is permitted on the Sabbath, there are cases where the reflection itself is forbidden by strict law — for example, one who strolls on the Sabbath in his field or at a workplace where his employees work during the week, in order to see what is needed there after the Sabbath. Even though he does not speak of it at all that day but only thinks it in his heart, this is forbidden by strict law, since the very act of going to a place he has no need of on the Sabbath itself reveals that he is going there to plan something forbidden to do on the Sabbath — for otherwise, what need would he have to go there specifically on that day? The same applies to one who strolls in the city where horses, donkeys, boats, or wagons are found, in order to choose what to hire tomorrow — this is forbidden for the same reason, even though he neither speaks nor performs any forbidden act that day itself.
takeaways: It is forbidden to go and stroll on the Sabbath at a place of business (such as a field, workplace, or animal market) with the intention of planning what to do after the Sabbath, even without speech or action — since the very act of going reveals the forbidden intention

paragraphs: Ap al gab demiddina im yosheb bimqomo umeharher baasaqayv muttar, mikkol maqom mishshum oneg shabbat, metzuvveh shello yechasheb bahem kelal, vihe roeh beenayv keillu melakto asuya, veyipneh libbo mikkol eseq shel chol, dehashshaa tzerika lekak ledabbeq machshabto beqono, leorer ahaba veyira besimcha rabba; vekol shekken heka deepshar sheyyihyeh lo mittok hirhur libbo baasaqayv tirdat leb o nidnud deaga, dela tzarik lihyot lo zeh beshabbat, ki tzarik beemet lihyot hashshabbat laadam menuchat shalom, hashqet ubetach, vekannizkar b"chesed leabraham" za"l; yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: Even though by strict law a person sitting in his place is permitted to reflect on his business on the Sabbath, nevertheless, for the sake of the commandment of delighting in the Sabbath, it is proper not to think about them at all, and to regard it as though all his work were already done, turning his heart completely away from weekday matters. The Sabbath is meant to bind one's thought to the Creator, to arouse love and awe with great joy, and all the more so one should refrain from reflecting on business when it might cause anxiety or worry — since such a thing has no place on the Sabbath, for the Sabbath is meant to be, for a person, true rest, tranquility, and security.
takeaways: Even when reflecting on business is permitted by strict law on the Sabbath, it is proper, for the sake of delighting in the Sabbath, to avoid it entirely and focus on closeness to God and inner rest
